title: Atom-selective spin-polarized transport in a charge-ordered altermagnet
authors: Liu Yang, Yuan-Yuan Jiang, Xiao-Yan Guo, Yi-Dong Liu, Xian-Zhe Chen, Wen-Jian Lu, Yu-Ping Sun, Ming Li, Ding-Fu Shao
abstract: Altermagnets provide a promising platform for spin-polarized transport without net magnetization, but their transport properties are usually discussed in terms of momentum-space spin splitting. Here, using first-principles calculations and quantum transport simulations, we show that the charge-ordered altermagnet $α$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$ exhibits a distinct form of real-space spin selectivity despite weak altermagnetic spin splitting near the Fermi level. The charge order creates inequivalent Fe$^{2+}$ and Fe$^{3+}$ sites within each sublattice, while the puckered C-type antiferromagnetic stacking suppresses inter-sublattice transport. As a result, electron and hole doping activate spin-polarized transport predominantly through Fe$^{3+}$- and Fe$^{2+}$-based channels, respectively. These atom-selective channels carry opposite spin polarizations on the two antiferromagnetic sublattices, giving rise to a globally compensated charge current with hidden Néel spin character. We further propose an all-in-one $α$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$ tunnel junction, where matching or mismatching atom-selective conduction channels yields orders-of-magnitude conductance modulation. Our findings establish a real-space design principle for atomically controlled spin functionality and spintronic devices.
summary: This work reveals that spin-polarized transport in the altermagnet $\alpha$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$ is governed by real-space, atom-selective conduction channels rather than just momentum-space splitting. By exploiting charge ordering to create distinct $	ext{Fe}^{2+}$ and $	ext{Fe}^{3+}$ sites, researchers show how doping can switch the current flow between these specific atomic pathways, enabling highly controllable spintronic devices.
main_problem: To investigate spin-polarized transport in altermagnets by moving beyond conventional momentum-space descriptions to focus on real-space spin selectivity.
main_result: The study demonstrates that charge ordering creates atom-selective conduction channels ($	ext{Fe}^{3+}$ vs $	ext{Fe}^{2+}$) which enable highly controllable, spin-polarized transport in the altermagnet $\alpha$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$. This mechanism allows for orders-of-magnitude conductance modulation via junction design.
method: The research employs first-principles calculations (DFT/GGA+U) combined with non-equilibrium Green’s function (NEGF) formalism to simulate quantum transport.
model_or_system: The system is the charge-ordered altermagnet $\alpha$-Fe$_2$PO$_5$, which possesses a puckered C-type antiferromagnetic stacking and exhibits inequivalent $	ext{Fe}^{2+}$ and $	ext{Fe}^{3+}$ sites due to charge ordering.
key_observables: Spin-resolved transmission coefficients ($\mathcal{T}^{\sigma}$), local conductance, spin polarization on sublattices, and junction conductance modulation (ON/OFF ratio).
important_parameters: Electron/hole doping levels ($n$ or $p$), the nature of the active atomic sites ($	ext{Fe}^{2+}$ vs $	ext{Fe}^{3+}$), and the degree of spin splitting near the Fermi level.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that real-space connectivity (atom selectivity) dictates transport properties even when momentum-space spin splitting is weak.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate crystal structures, band/DOS showing weak splitting, constant-energy surfaces for spin states, and schematic representations of bond-resolved transmission ($\mathcal{T}$ vs $\mathcal{T}^{\sigma}$) under different doping conditions in a tunnel junction model.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the limitations of momentum-space analysis to identifying real-space charge/spin selectivity due to site inequivalence, demonstrating this through transport calculations, and finally proposing an all-in-one tunnel junction device concept based on channel matching.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the core concept—controlling quantum transport via engineered local chemical potential (doping) to select specific atomic pathways—is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems where boundary conditions or site chemistry dictate coherence and current flow.
